extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, parties seeking mandamus relief from Federal Circuit, and PTO practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation of petitions for writs of mandamus seeking to vacate or compel reconsideration of PTO decisions declining institution of inter partes review (IPR). Focuses on the legal standards a petitioner must meet and the PTO's permissible grounds (e.g., 'settled expectations') for denying institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandamus relief requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner seeking mandamus relief must ordinarily satisfy three requirements: (1) a clear and indisputable right to relief; (2) a lack of adequate alternative means to obtain the relief sought; and (3) a showing that issuance of the writ is appropriate under the circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the Cheney standard (Cheney v. U.S. Dist. Ct. for D.C., 542 U.S. 367, 380–81 (2004)). Petitioners must demonstrate all three elements to obtain mandamus; failure on any prong is dispositive. The court applied the same framework as in In re Cambridge Industries USA Inc., and relied on precedent including Cuozzo Speed Techs. v. Lee and Thryv, Inc. v. Click-To-Call Techs., LP when assessing whether petitioners met their burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO consideration: 'settled expectations' as a basis to decline IPR institution
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTO may decline to institute IPR by considering that challenged patents have been in force for years, creating 'strong settled expectations' (here: approximately nine, twelve, and twelve years). The PTO noted petitioners had not 'provide[d] any persuasive reasoning why [IPR] is an appropriate use of [PTAB] resources.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When patents have long been in force, 'settled expectations' is a legitimate factor supporting denial of institution absent persuasive justification for disturbing those expectations. Non-constitutional challenges to the PTO's consideration of settled expectations do not by themselves establish a clear and indisputable right to mandamus relief (citing Cuozzo, Thryv, and Cambridge). Parties should supply persuasive, case-specific reasons if asking the PTO to institute IPR despite lengthy patent maturity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colorable constitutional challenge requires identification of property-rights or retroactivity concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: To press a constitutional challenge to the PTO's denial of IPR institution, petitioners must identify the kind of property rights or retroactivity concerns that might give rise to a colorable constitutional claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent an identified property-right or retroactivity problem, a petitioner cannot establish the constitutional basis necessary to show a clear and indisputable right to relief. The court here held petitioners failed to identify such rights/concerns, and for that reason the constitutional argument did not support mandamus.
